Case study · 01 / 04

Unbolt — an AR repair companion for DIY mechanics.

Client Unbolt (via Hyper Studio)
Role Embedded Product Manager
Year 2023
Focus Discovery · MVP scoping · Prototype
01 — Project overview

Working with founders at Hyper.

At Hyper, I embedded inside early-stage startups as their product manager — somewhere between a co-founder and a consultant. My job was to help founders with a strong sense of what they wanted to build figure out what they needed to build first.

And while the role sat under "product", I stayed close to the craft — driving the UX and contributing directly to the UI, from brand and visual hierarchy down to reworking individual screens myself.

It was 0→1 work: taking a raw idea all the way through discovery, scoping and design into a working prototype — something concrete enough to validate the concept with real users and put in front of investors to raise.

Unbolt's founder, Omar, arrived with a clear idea — an AR-powered app guiding DIY mechanics through repairs step by step — and real conviction. My role was to shape that energy into something a developer could build and an investor could believe in, within a realistic scope.

Jump to the prototype ↓
02 — Discovery

Starting with a workshop, not a wireframe.

I kicked the project off by running a discovery workshop with the founder to unpack the idea. We focused on the core problem to solve, the target users and their behaviours, and the envisioned solution — followed by an initial feature dump covering everything from AR guidance and diagnostics to a marketplace and community.

The workshop aligned us on the vision, but it also surfaced a familiar 0→1 challenge: too many ideas, not enough focus.

03 — Exploration

Mapping what already exists before adding to it.

I translated the workshop outputs into a structured exploration phase in FigJam — brainstorming sessions with the commercial team, competitor analysis (YouTube, Haynes, AllData), market and user-behaviour research, and mapping how users currently solve the problem.

The goal here was simple: understand what already exists, and find where Unbolt could genuinely add value rather than reinvent it.

04 — Users

Three user types, one shared challenge.

Before scoping features, we agreed on who Unbolt was for — and, crucially, who it wasn’t. The brief called for a tool that could meet a range of confidence levels without watering any of them down. Three archetypes shaped every subsequent decision.

Primary · 01

DIY car enthusiasts.

Passionate individuals immersed in automotive culture, seeking authoritative and comprehensive guidance to tackle complex repair projects with confidence and enhance their hands-on experience.

Drive
Hands-on confidence
Context
Home garage,full tool set
Need
Authoritative guidance

“If I'm going to take it apart myself, I want to know I'm doing it right.”

Secondary · 02

Tech-savvy car owners.

Forward-thinking individuals who embrace technology to demystify vehicle maintenance, keen on a deeper, more interactive understanding of their car's mechanics and potential issues.

Drive
Understanding the machine
Context
Phone-first, OBD-curious
Need
Interactive insight

“I want to know what's actually going on under the bonnet.

Edge · 03

Amateur DIYers & mechanics.

Dedicated hobbyists eager to refine their mechanical prowess, craving precise, user-friendly instructions and diagnostics to elevate their repair skill set and tackle more challenging projects.

Drive
Skill progression
Context
Driveway or workshop
Need
Precise step-by-step

“Show me exactly what to do — and I'll be ready for the next job up.”

05 — Problem

A fragmented experience for people who want to fix their own cars.

DIY mechanics have no reliable, unified place to turn. The result is a lack of confidence at exactly the moment it matters most — under the bonnet with a spanner in hand. Four recurring frustrations shaped the brief.

Information

Manuals are outdated and generic.

Printed guides cover the make but rarely the specific model year, engine variant or trim that's sitting on the driveway.

01
Trust

YouTube is hit and miss.

Quality varies wildly. Users spend time cross-checking three videos before they feel safe touching anything.

02
Orientation

"Which part is this, exactly?"

Engine bays look nothing like the diagrams. Identifying the right component in real life is the first stumbling block.

03
Confidence

No way to check progress mid-repair.

Halfway through a job, users can't tell if they've done a step correctly. Doubt creeps in — and tools get put down.

04
06 — Prioritisation

From too many features to just 8.

With a long list of potential features, the job was to narrow down what mattered most. I pressure-tested every idea against two questions: does this help a user complete their first repair? And does this make Unbolt meaningfully different?

At Hyper, we also worked within a deliberate constraint — if a feature didn't earn a screen in the prototype, it wasn't ready. That forced the move from a broad vision to a focused, testable set, and gave us a way to say no without losing the founder's bigger ambitions.

Artefact — Feature prioritisation table 11 features · 8 included · 3 deferred

Features assessed during scoping. MVP column reflects what was included in the prototype handed to investors.

Feature Decision Rationale
Personalised dashboard MVP Vehicle overview surfacing OBD-detected issues with error codes, plus a quick-launch into AR-guided repair — the core entry point that helps users understand their car at a glance.
Diagnostic tool integration MVP Connects with OBD scanners for real-time diagnostics, interpreting codes and offering actionable recommendations — turning complex vehicle data into something understandable.
Vehicle-specific repair guides MVP Bespoke instructions for the detected error, tailored to the exact make, model and year — ensuring guidance is precise and relevant to the user's car.
AR repair visualisations MVP Overlays digital instructions onto the vehicle through the device camera, providing intuitive visual guides and interactive elements for each repair step.
Repair tracking tools MVP Detailed task lists with the ability to mark steps complete — helping users organise repair projects and keep automotive work on track.
Cloud data storage MVP Premium-tier secure storage for repair history, diagnostics and personalised settings — accessible from any device so important data is always within reach.
Spare parts & consumables recommendations MVP Tailored suggestions for parts needed for specific repairs, directing users to trusted suppliers — simplifying sourcing and ensuring compatibility.
Automotive service centre recommendations MVP Recommends professional service centres when a task is too complex or risky for DIY — a reliable fallback so users always have a trusted route forward.
Real-time inventory tracking Future For professional mechanics — live stock levels and low-stock notifications. Outside the consumer MVP scope but valuable for a later B2B tier.
Team collaboration Future Task assignment, shared project info and real-time team comms for workshops. Deferred until the consumer experience is validated.
Third-party software integrations Future Hooks into accounting and project management tools used by professional mechanics. Requires partnerships and scale — not viable at MVP stage.
07 — User flow

Mapping the path from problem to repair.

Once the feature set was agreed, I mapped the end-to-end user journey. The flow had to feel logical and low-anxiety — a first-time user shouldn't have to think about what to do next at any point. Starting with vehicle setup and ending with a confirmed repair gives the experience a clear beginning, middle, and end.

08 — Wireframes

Designing the structure, not the surface.

My contribution to the wireframes was focused on structure and information hierarchy — what each screen needed to communicate, in what order, and why. Every screen in the MVP flow was mine to think through, from first-run splash to success: laying out the navigation, defining the states, and making sure each decision a user had to make was the right size for that moment in the journey.

The goal was to give the design team a clear, opinionated foundation — not a blank canvas — so the visual work could focus on expression rather than untangling the logic.

01 · Dashboard

Vehicle status, at a glance.

The home screen surfaces vehicle make and model, mileage and VIN, alongside diagnostic results from the OBD scan, active repair projects, and consumables tracking — giving the user a complete operational picture before they start any work.

02 · Selected Project

The operational heart of the app.

A detailed overview of the user's car, including diagnostic issues identified via the OBD scan with specific error codes — and a prominent option to launch the AR-guided repair journey.

03 · Selected Step

Problem, parts, repair preview.

Selecting an issue from the dashboard surfaces a comprehensive description of the problem, a step-by-step preview of the repair, the necessary spare parts and consumables with direct links to purchase, and instructions for validating success at the end.

04 · AR Repair

Scan, highlight and repair — in one immersive flow.

The AR experience runs end-to-end across three modes: scanning prompts the user to point their camera at the vehicle for precise component identification; highlighting uses visual overlays to draw attention directly to the faulty part; and repair instructions walk the user through each step like a virtual mechanic, with detailed visual and verbal cues.

05 · Back to Selected Step

Tracking, parts and proof.

Returned to once the AR guide closes. Revisits the problem, surfaces a checklist for marking steps complete, catalogues required parts with a purchase route, and integrates an image upload tool for user reference — concluding with a verification guide and a button to confirm the repair is complete.

06 · Success Screen

Completion, celebrated.

Once the user marks the repair as complete, this celebratory interface confirms a successful repair — encouraging users to share their achievement on social media.

09 — Visual design

The same flow, rendered in the Unbolt brand we built.

The hi-fi visuals were produced with Hyper's design team, but I stayed hands-on with the UI throughout — driving the direction on branding, colour, typography and visual hierarchy where the designers were less close to the product, feeding back on every iteration, and frequently reworking the screens myself to keep the interface true to how the product needed to work.

10 — Outcome

A prototype the founder could put in front of investors.

The Unbolt prototype went on to be used in investor pitches. That's the metric that matters most at this stage — not whether every feature was perfect, but whether the product was coherent enough to communicate the vision and credible enough to inspire confidence in what could be built next.

8 → 7

8 Features designed in 7 screens that each had to earn their place in the prototype.

Used in pitches

The prototype was handed off and carried into investor meetings — the measure of success at this stage.

1 focused  MVP

A coherent first version for Omar to validate and build, instead of twenty half-sketched directions.

11 — Key learnings

What I'm taking into the next one.

Looking back, the most valuable thing I contributed wasn't any individual screen. It was the discipline of the scoping process itself — helping a founder with a big idea understand that a focused first version isn't a compromise. It's the thing that makes everything else possible.

No. 01

A focused first version is not a compromise.

Cutting scope wasn't cutting corners. Naming the one thing the prototype had to prove, and protecting it from everything else, was what made the rest of the design decisions possible.

No. 02

Process is the deliverable when the path is unclear.

The most useful thing I left behind wasn't a screen — it was a repeatable way of asking "what does this version need to prove, and to whom?" that the founder could carry into the next round.

No. 03

Hierarchy is the brief for the visual team.

Spending time on information structure and flow logic up front meant the design team could focus on expression — not untangling what each screen needed to communicate.
